citation: Panagioti M, Panagopoulou E, Bower P, Lewith G, Kontopantelis E, Chew-Graham C, Dawson S, van Marwijk H, Geraghty K, Esmail A. Controlled Interventions to Reduce Burnout in Physicians: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2017;177(2):195-205. Published online 5 December 2016. doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2016.7674
source_tier: Peer-reviewed (systematic review and meta-analysis, JAMA Internal Medicine)

exact_quotes: 'Interventions were associated with small significant reductions in burnout (standardized mean difference [SMD] = −0.29; 95% CI, −0.42 to −0.16; equal to a drop of 3 points on the emotional exhaustion domain of the Maslach Burnout Inventory above change in the controls).' (Abstract, Results)
'Twenty independent comparisons from 19 studies were included in the meta-analysis (n = 1550 physicians; mean [SD] age, 40.3 [9.5] years; 49% male).' (Abstract, Results)

'Subgroup analyses suggested significantly improved effects for organization-directed interventions (SMD = −0.45; 95% CI, −0.62 to −0.28) compared with physician-directed interventions (SMD = −0.18; 95% CI, −0.32 to −0.03).' (Abstract, Results)
'The effects of organization-directed interventions were significantly larger than the effects of physician-directed interventions (Cohen Q = 4.15, P = .04).' (Results, Types of Interventions)
'The strongest evidence for effectiveness was found for organization-directed interventions, but these interventions were rare.' (Key Points, Findings)

'Within the category of organization-directed interventions, 5 studies evaluated simple workload interventions that focused on rescheduling hourly shifts and reducing workload. Only 3 studies tested more extensive organization-directed interventions incorporating discussion meetings to enhance teamwork and leadership, structural changes, and elements of physician interventions such as communication skills training and mindfulness.' (Results, Characteristics of Interventions)
'The majority of organization-directed interventions that we included in the analyses introduced simple reductions in the workload or schedule changes.' (Discussion, Implications)

'Those that combined several elements such as structural changes, fostering communication between members of the health care team, and cultivating a sense of teamwork and job control tended to be the most effective in reducing burnout. However, such intense organization-directed interventions were rare and were not evaluated widely.' (Discussion, Implications)
'At present, the low quality of the research evidence does not allow firm practical recommendations, but we offer some insights for research and clinical directions.' (Discussion, Implications)

'The included studies differed significantly in terms of content of interventions, study design and/or quality, and length of follow-up that limit the extent to which broad conclusions can be drawn about the overall effectiveness of physician interventions.' (Discussion, Strengths and Limitations)
'subgroup analyses should be interpreted cautiously because other, uncontrolled differences between studies might account for the results.' (Discussion, Strengths and Limitations)

'Physician-directed interventions led to very small significant reductions in burnout. We found no evidence that the content (eg, mindfulness, communicational, educational components) or intensity of these interventions might increase the derived benefits...' (Discussion)

'If burnout is a problem of whole health care systems, it is less likely to be effectively minimized by solely intervening at the individual level. It requires an organization-embedded approach.' (Discussion)

'physicians expected to deal with burnout individually and remotely from their practicing organization might view physician-directed interventions as a personal responsibility (or blame themselves for being less “resilient”)...' (Discussion)
'This finding provides support for the view that burnout is a problem of the whole health care organization, rather than individuals.' (Abstract, Conclusions)
date_and_recency: Published online 5 December 2016; print February 2017 (vol 177, no 2). Literature searched from inception to 31 May 2016. Included studies span 2005 to 2016. Pre-dates pandemic-era burnout work and any software or AI context.
key_claims: Controlled interventions to reduce physician burnout produce small but significant reductions in emotional exhaustion (SMD -0.29). Organisation-directed interventions (SMD -0.45, a 'medium' effect) beat physician-directed ones (SMD -0.18, 'very small'), and the difference is statistically significant (Q=4.15, P=.04). Authors read this as support for burnout being a problem of the organisation, not the individual. The strongest organisation-directed approaches combined structural change, team communication and job control, but were rare. The authors also say the low quality of evidence does not allow firm practical recommendations.
headline_figures: Pooled effect: SMD = -0.29 (95% CI -0.42 to -0.16), I2 = 30%. Back-transformed emotional exhaustion: 15.1 intervention vs 17.9 control (assuming SD 8.97), described as a 3-point drop on the MBI emotional exhaustion subscale.

Organisation-directed: SMD = -0.45 (95% CI -0.62 to -0.28), I2 = 8%; back-transformed EE 13.9 vs 17.9 control. Eight comparisons in Figure 3 (Ali 2011, Garland 2012, Linzer 2015a and 2015b, Lucas 2012, Parshuram 2015, Shea 2014, West 2014).
Physician-directed: SMD = -0.18 (95% CI -0.32 to -0.03), I2 = 11%; back-transformed EE 16.2 vs 17.9 control. 12 studies (60%).
Sample: 19 studies, 20 independent comparisons, 1550 physicians, mean age 40.3 (SD 9.5), 49% male. 18 comparisons were RCTs (95%), 2 controlled before-after. 8 studies in the US (42%).
Of the organisation-directed group: 5 studies tested simple workload or rescheduling interventions, 3 tested more extensive multi-component interventions.
Experienced physicians (mean 5+ years) SMD -0.37 vs less experienced SMD -0.27; difference not significant (P = .34). Primary care SMD -0.39 vs secondary care -0.24; not significant (P = .48).
Secondary outcomes: depersonalisation SMD -0.21; personal accomplishment SMD 0.30. Low-risk-of-bias studies only: SMD -0.32.
Intervention duration 2 weeks to 9 months; follow-up 1 day to 18 months. No funnel plot asymmetry (Egger P = .11).
sample_unit_and_population: 1550 physicians across 19 controlled studies (20 comparisons) in primary care (7 studies), secondary care including ICU, oncology, surgery and residents (10), and mixed (2). Physicians had to make up at least 70% of the sample (one study retained at 67%). Not software engineers. Studies mostly had residents/interns or practising doctors working shifts; no knowledge workers outside medicine.
observed_vs_stated: Stated. Burnout was self-reported on a questionnaire; all but one study used the Maslach Burnout Inventory, and the meta-analysis used only the emotional exhaustion subscale. No physiological or behavioural measures.
what_it_measures_or_defines: Defines burnout as 'a syndrome consisting of emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and a diminished sense of personal accomplishment, which is primarily driven by workplace stressors.' Core outcome is the emotional exhaustion domain of the MBI, chosen because it is 'considered the most central aspect of burnout'. Depersonalisation and personal accomplishment were analysed only as sensitivity analyses.
mechanism_or_cause: Leading drivers named: 'excessive workload, imbalance between job demands and skills, a lack of job control, and prolonged work stress.' Authors describe a shift from viewing burnout as an individual problem to one of the organisation, 'rooted in issues related to working environment and organizational culture'. Their reading of the larger organisation-directed effect is that burnout is rooted in organisational coherence, so individual-level interventions alone are less likely to work.
interventions_and_effects: Physician-directed (12 studies, 60%): mindfulness-based stress reduction, communication skills training, stress management, self-care workshops, debriefing/discussion groups, exercise. Pooled SMD -0.18, 'very small'. Authors found no evidence that content or intensity changed the benefit. Organisation-directed (8 comparisons): mostly workload and schedule changes (shift rotation length, intensivist staffing schedules, protected sleep time for interns, overnight shift length, e.g. Ali, Lucas, Parshuram, Shea); 3 studies were multi-component (teamwork, quality improvement, communication, workflow changes, protected paid time for facilitated discussion groups, e.g. Linzer 2015, West 2014). Pooled SMD -0.45. Authors say the multi-component ones tended to be most effective but were rare. Caution: the headline 'organisation-directed' effect is dominated by Lucas 2012 (weight 48.7% within the subgroup, SMD -0.44). Individual organisation-directed effects ranged from -0.10 (Parshuram) to -0.98 (Linzer 2015b). Note West 2014 was classed organisation-directed although it is built from mindfulness and discussion-group elements with institution-funded protected time.
transfer_to_software_teams: Indirect. All evidence is from physicians in clinical settings (shift-based, patient-facing, many residents). No software engineers. The logic that workload and schedule changes and team-level structural change beat individual coping training is plausible to carry across, but the specific effect sizes should not be assumed to transfer. Use as medical-profession evidence about the relative value of organisational versus individual remedies.
limitations_stated: Quotes: 'The included studies differed significantly in terms of content of interventions, study design and/or quality, and length of follow-up that limit the extent to which broad conclusions can be drawn about the overall effectiveness of physician interventions.' 'subgroup analyses should be interpreted cautiously because other, uncontrolled differences between studies might account for the results.' 'At present, the low quality of the research evidence does not allow firm practical recommendations.' Also: organisation-directed interventions 'were rare and were not evaluated widely'; 'other unexamined factors at the process of the intervention delivery or at the participant level might account for the observed differences'. Authors also note gray literature was excluded, and the 3-point back-transformation was done 'under certain assumptions'. Stated strengths: 20 comparisons, low to moderate heterogeneity (I2 30%), no funnel plot asymmetry.
counter_evidence: Authors concede the subgroup comparison (organisation vs physician) is not randomised and could be confounded by other study differences; the P value is borderline (.04). The organisation-directed subgroup is only 8 comparisons and is dominated by one study (Lucas 2012, 48.7% weight). Most organisation-directed interventions were workload or schedule tweaks, so the result does not show that culture or system redesign works. Experience and setting subgroup differences were not significant. Follow-up was often short (many post-intervention only). Studies were not selected for people with high burnout (none targeted a severity level). Later literature on physician burnout interventions is outside this source.
verification_status: All figures and quotes checked against the opened PDF text: 19 studies / 20 comparisons / 1550 physicians [confirmed], pooled SMD -0.29 [confirmed], organisation-directed -0.45 and physician-directed -0.18 [confirmed], Q=4.15 P=.04 [confirmed], 5 simple workload studies plus 3 extensive [confirmed in text], 'majority of organization-directed interventions ... simple reductions in the workload or schedule changes' [confirmed verbatim]. The count of 8 organisation-directed comparisons is derived from Figure 3 (the Methods text says 5 + 3 studies; Linzer 2015 contributes two comparisons) and the table classification of Ali 2011 is garbled in the text extraction, so which of the 5 simple-workload studies are which is [uncertain] but does not affect the headline claims.
usable_claim: A 2017 JAMA Internal Medicine meta-analysis of 19 controlled studies (1,550 physicians) found interventions produced small reductions in burnout (SMD -0.29, about 3 points on the MBI emotional exhaustion scale). Interventions aimed at the organisation did better (SMD -0.45) than those aimed at the individual physician (SMD -0.18), and the authors read that as support for burnout being an organisational problem. Most of the organisation-directed interventions were simple workload or schedule changes, and the authors say the evidence is too low in quality for firm practical recommendations. The evidence is from doctors, not software engineers.
do_not_use: Do not say the organisation-directed effect proves system or culture change works: most were rescheduling or workload cuts, and the fuller multi-component programmes were only 3 studies. Do not present -0.45 as a causal head-to-head result (the subgroup comparison is non-randomised and borderline at P=.04). Do not describe the individual-level effect as zero; it was small but significant. Do not claim the findings apply to software engineers. Do not claim the paper says mindfulness 'doesn't work'. Do not quote the 3-point drop as clinically decisive; the authors say 'important benefits' but also 'low quality' evidence.
